items.name: Chemistry -- CONTROL r0
items.response:
Distinguishing a genuine rearrangement of an intended intermediate from an artifact introduced with impure reagents is a matter of structure first and provenance second, and the two lines of work use quite different tools. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction establishes the atomic connectivity of the unexpected product, settling without argument what has actually been isolated from the flask; combustion elemental analysis, by contrast, determines the connectivity of atoms within a molecule. High-resolution mass spectrometry distinguishes constitutional isomers by their exact masses, which makes it the fastest way to ask whether the new material is a rearranged isomer of the intended product or something structurally unrelated to it.

After the diffraction work has fixed the structure, attention turns to the history of the individual atoms. Isotopic labeling of a single carbon in the starting material allows the atom to be tracked into the unexpected product, so that its fate, rather than merely the final connectivity, becomes observable. Unlike combustion analysis, carbon-13 labeling experiments reveal whether bonds in the carbon skeleton migrate during the reaction. In the case at hand, that labeling experiment resulted in the carbon-13 label occupying a different position in the product than in the starting material; that is, the isotopic label migrated to a new site over the course of the reaction.

A skeletal migration within a single molecule must still be separated from pathways in which fragments are exchanged between molecules, and the standard control for that question is well established. A crossover experiment is run with two differently labeled substrates in the same vessel, and precisely because the labels are brought together in one pot in this way, the appearance of mixed-label products indicates an intermolecular pathway. GC-MS analysis of the starting material detects volatile impurities present below one percent. Spiking the starting material with a suspected impurity tests whether that impurity generates the unexpected product.

That spiking trial leads straight to a further control, in that repeating the reaction with starting material from a second supplier tests whether the outcome is batch-dependent. With the candidate impurity identified and the material purified, the decisive comparison takes a very simple form: either the reaction run with recrystallized starting material produced the unexpected product, or the reaction run with recrystallized starting material produced none of the unexpected product, and exactly one of those two outcomes, never both, will be found at the bench. Which one is observed is what actually closes the case, since no amount of spectroscopy performed on the isolated product can by itself say where that product came from.
